passage: I'm Asif. Before the maths test, Karthik sat next to me wringing his hands, one over the other, again and again. I thought he must be nervous. I almost said nothing because I didn't want to make it worse. Then I whispered, “You okay?” He said, “I always forget the formulas.” I said, “Me too. Want to go through the area one quickly?” We did it for two minutes, and his hands stopped. I don't know if that was the only reason, because it was cold in the room too. But it helped a bit.

qa.q: What was Karthik doing with his hands before the test?
qa.a: He was wringing his hands, one over the other, again and again.

qa.q: What did Asif think Karthik was feeling, and how sure can he be?
qa.a: He thought Karthik was nervous, and Karthik said he always forgets the formulas, which fits. Asif admits he cannot be sure, since the room was also cold.

qa.q: What small step helped Karthik?
qa.a: Asif asked quietly if he was okay and offered to go through the formula together, which gave Karthik something concrete to do.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when Asif whispered to him?
qa.a: Probably relieved that somebody noticed and did not make a fuss, and less alone with his worry.

grounding: A child sees a classmate wring the hands before a test, reads nervousness, and offers a friendly word.

passage: Note from Hafsa, Class 5 teacher. Before the spelling test I saw Noor wringing her hands under the desk. I could not tell if she was nervous or just cold from the fan. I bent down and asked quietly how she felt about the test. She said, “I keep thinking I'll go blank.” I told her she could take a slow breath and begin with the words she knows best. Her hands loosened. I did not tell the class. I will check in with her privately before the next test and ask what helped.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa see Noor wringing her hands?
qa.a: She saw Noor wringing her hands under the desk.

qa.q: What was Noor most likely feeling, and what else could explain her hands?
qa.a: Most likely she was nervous about going blank in the test, as she told Hafsa. Cold from the fan could also have made her wring her hands.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do that helped, and what will she do next?
qa.a: She asked quietly and privately and offered a way to start, and she will check in before the next test to ask what helped.

qa.q: How might Noor have felt when Hafsa bent down to ask?
qa.a: Probably relieved that it was done quietly, without the other children noticing. She was able to say her worry in words.

grounding: Wringing hands before a test suggests nervousness though it does not prove it; a friendly word helps.

passage:
In the colony, Tenzin posed for a photo with his cousin's friends, flashing a V-sign with his palm turned toward himself. Binita, who had just come back from London, grimaced. “In Britain, the V with the palm facing in is rude. Palm out is the peace sign.”
“Really? I meant it as friendly!”
“I know. But be careful.”
“What about the OK sign?”
“In some countries that's rude too. And the thumbs-up isn't friendly everywhere.”
Tenzin lowered his hand. “So I'll ask before I use them abroad.”

qa.q: Which V-sign did Binita say is rude in Britain?
qa.a: She said the V with the palm facing in is rude in Britain.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when Binita told him about the V-sign?
qa.a: Surprised and probably a bit embarrassed, since he meant it as friendly. He then became careful and curious, asking about the other signs.

qa.q: What would you advise Tenzin before he travels?
qa.a: Ask a local, a teacher or someone who has been there about gestures, and use words and a smile when unsure.

qa.q: How might a British classmate see Tenzin's backward V?
qa.a: As rude, even though Tenzin means it kindly. They might be taken aback until he explained.

grounding: Thumbs-up, OK and V-sign can be friendly in one place and rude in another; care with travel is wise.

passage:
“Lokesh, why didn't you give the waiter the OK sign?” asked Shankar. “You always do.”
“Uncle told me that in some countries the OK sign means something rude. So I just said thank you.”
“Really?”
“Yes. And a backward V is rude in Britain.”
“Then what do I use?”
“Words and a smile. Or watch what other people do.”
Shankar laughed. “That's much safer.”
“Uncle also said thumbs-up is friendly here, but I'll check first when we travel.”

qa.q: What did Lokesh say to the waiter instead of using the OK sign?
qa.a: He said thank you.

qa.q: What might Lokesh be feeling when he chooses words over the OK sign, and what else might explain it?
qa.a: He is probably being careful, since Uncle warned him that signs can mean something rude in some countries. He may also enjoy knowing something Shankar does not.

qa.q: What would you advise a child who is new to a place?
qa.a: Watch what other people do, use words and a smile, and ask a friendly person what a sign means before using it.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel when he learns about these signs?
qa.a: Surprised and a little amused, and probably willing to be more careful.

grounding: Thumbs-up, OK and V-sign can be friendly in one place and rude in another; care with travel is wise.

passage:
At Dadaji's flat, Anand hung back by the door.
“Anand, greet Dadaji,” said Disha, his mother.
“Do I have to touch his feet?”
“Only if you want to. You can also fold your hands and say namaste.”
Dadaji chuckled from his chair. “A warm hello is enough, beta. Come here.”
Anand looked at the floor, then walked over and bent to touch Dadaji's feet. Dadaji put a hand lightly on his head. “Blessings. How is school?”
“Good,” said Anand, smiling. “I got a star.”

qa.q: Who told Anand he could fold his hands instead of touching feet?
qa.a: Disha, his mother, told him he could fold his hands and say namaste.

qa.q: What might Anand have felt when he hung back and asked if he had to touch feet, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably shy or unsure about the custom, and perhaps a little pressured. He might also just have been nervous about meeting Dadaji.

qa.q: How did the adults respond in a way that respects the child?
qa.a: Disha and Dadaji made it a choice, saying a warm hello is enough, so Anand touched the feet by his own decision.

qa.q: How might Dadaji see the touching of his feet?
qa.a: As a mark of respect and a chance to bless his grandchild, and he also said a warm hello would do, so he did not seem to demand it.

grounding: Touching elders' feet is respect and a way to receive blessings, and a child is never forced into touch.

passage: I'm Suraj. Every morning I touch my grandfather's feet. It's my way of saying thank you, and he blesses me. When my friend Wasim came over, he greeted my grandmother by putting a hand on his chest and saying, “Assalamu alaikum.” She smiled and said “Wa alaikum assalam.” Then she asked, “May I bless you too?” Wasim nodded, and she touched his head gently. Later she told me, “Respect lives in the heart, not only in the feet.” I thought about that. Wasim's way and mine are different, and both are respectful.

qa.q: What does Wasim say when he greets Suraj's grandmother?
qa.a: He puts a hand on his chest and says “Assalamu alaikum.”

qa.q: What does Suraj feel about touching his grandfather's feet?
qa.a: It is his way of saying thank you, and he seems to value the blessing. He also comes to see that other ways of showing respect are just as good.

qa.q: What did the grandmother do that respected Wasim's choice?
qa.a: She asked “May I bless you too?” and waited for his nod before touching his head, and she accepted his greeting in his own way.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel about being greeted by the grandmother in that way?
qa.a: Probably welcomed and respected, since she answered his greeting warmly and asked before touching him.

grounding: Touching elders' feet is a cultural sign of respect, and respect can be shown in other ways with consent.

passage: I'm Keerthana, and when I get excited telling a story, my brother Sahil holds his palms out and pushes them down gently. At first I thought it meant, “Stop, you're annoying.” Then I looked at his face. He was smiling. “Slow down, I want to hear it properly,” he said. So I took a breath and told it slowly. Yesterday my classmate did the same gesture with a stiff face and said, “Calm down.” That felt different, like she didn't want to hear me at all. Same hands, but the face and voice make it kind or not.

qa.q: What does Sahil do with his palms when Keerthana gets excited?
qa.a: He holds his palms out and pushes them down gently.

qa.q: What did Keerthana first think Sahil's gesture meant, and what changed her mind?
qa.a: She first thought it meant he found her annoying. His smile and his words, “Slow down, I want to hear it properly”, changed her mind.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do when a classmate uses the gesture with a stiff face?
qa.a: Ask calmly whether she is being too loud or say that she would like to finish her story, rather than assuming rejection.

qa.q: How might the classmate see her own gesture?
qa.a: Perhaps as a simple way to ask for calm, without noticing that her stiff face made it feel dismissive.

grounding: Palms pressing down mean slow down; kind or dismissive depends on the face and tone that come with it.

passage: Note from Raghav, sports coach. Hemant talks loudly in the huddle when he's excited. I press my palms gently downward with a smile, and he now lowers his voice. Today I saw a teammate make the same gesture with a flat face in the middle of a game. Hemant went silent and stared at his shoes. I asked him privately afterwards. He said, “It felt like he thought I was silly.” I explained that the same gesture can be kind or dismissive and that the face and tone tell you which. Next practice I will invite the two of them to talk it through.

qa.q: What does Raghav do with his palms to get Hemant to lower his voice?
qa.a: He presses his palms gently downward with a smile.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he went silent after the teammate's gesture, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed, since he said it felt like the teammate thought he was silly. He might also have been just focusing on the game, but he told Raghav how it felt.

qa.q: What did Raghav do that helped, and what will he do next?
qa.a: He asked Hemant privately and explained that face and tone show whether the gesture is kind, and he will invite the two boys to talk it through.

qa.q: How might the teammate have meant his gesture?
qa.a: Possibly as a simple, quick request for calm in the middle of a game, without noticing his flat face looked dismissive.

grounding: Palms pressing down mean slow down; a kind or dismissive reading depends on the face and tone.

subtype: Time-out gesture and pausing a game [Expressing]
passage: Note from Usha, coach. In today's football game a quarrel started over whether the ball had crossed the line. Vishal made a T with his hands and called, “Time out! Can we check the rule?” Both teams paused. We looked at the rule together and the argument ended. Later, in a different game, another child made the T when his team was behind. His friends said, “You just want to stop because you're losing,” and he went red. I did not scold him. I asked him what he needed, and he said he was upset. We took a short break and he rejoined.

qa.q: What did Vishal ask the players to check when he made a T?
qa.a: He asked them to check the rule.

qa.q: What was the second child probably feeling when he made the T, and what did his friends assume?
qa.a: Probably upset about being behind, as he later told Usha. His friends assumed he wanted to stop because he was losing, which was partly true and partly missing his distress.

qa.q: What did Usha do that worked with the second child?
qa.a: She did not scold him and asked what he needed, so he could say he was upset, and a short break helped him rejoin.

qa.q: How might Vishal's teammates see his T compared with the second child's?
qa.a: They probably saw Vishal's as honest, since he wanted to check a rule, while the second child's looked like dodging a loss.

grounding: A T with the hands pauses a game or quarrel; used honestly it lowers conflict, but peers notice when it dodges a loss.

subtype: Time-out gesture and pausing a game [Expressing]
passage: Pankaj's diary, Sunday. Made a T with my hands today when Uma was about to win at Ludo. She said, “That's not fair. You always call time-out when you're behind!” I said I needed to check the rule about sixes, but honestly I wasn't sure. I felt hot in the face. I think she's partly right. I was scared to lose again. So I told her sorry and said we could keep playing. She said okay and then she won anyway, and it wasn't as bad as I thought. Next time I'll call time-out only when there really is a rule to clear up.

qa.q: Which game were Pankaj and Uma playing?
qa.a: They were playing Ludo.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when he made the T, and what does he admit?
qa.a: He was scared of losing again and felt hot in the face. He admits Uma is partly right, even though he said it was about the rule.

qa.q: What could Pankaj try next time he feels upset in a game?
qa.a: Use the time-out only for real rule questions, and say plainly if he is upset and needs a moment.

qa.q: How might Uma feel when Pankaj apologises and keeps playing?
qa.a: Probably relieved, since her complaint was heard, and happy that the game goes on. She might also feel a little proud of winning.

grounding: A T with the hands pauses a game; using it to dodge a loss is noticed by peers, while honest use lowers conflict.

subtype: Reading a speaker's gestures for meaning [Interpreting]
passage: Madhav Sir stood in the schoolyard with a bucket of water beside the dry drain. “Last monsoon the water in the well rose this high,” he said, sweeping his hand up above his head. Darshan's eyes followed the hand. That was taller than he was! But Sir's arm was stretched wide in the way he always tells stories. Darshan raised his hand. “Sir, is that really how high it was?” Sir laughed. “Good question. My hand was showing the mood. It was really up to here,” and he tapped his waist.

qa.q: What was next to the dry drain?
qa.a: A bucket of water was beside the dry drain.

qa.q: What was Darshan thinking when he asked if that was really how high the water had been?
qa.a: He wanted to check the meaning, since the gesture looked bigger than he expected and he knew Sir stretches his arm when telling stories. He may also have been a little worried he was misunderstanding.

qa.q: What would help pupils read a teacher's gestures for meaning?
qa.a: Watch the gesture and the words together, and ask a follow-up question, as Darshan did, when the picture seems exaggerated.

qa.q: How might Madhav Sir see his own gesture?
qa.a: As a lively way to make the story vivid, without realising it could mislead. He was pleased Darshan asked.

grounding: A pupil reads a teacher's hand gestures for size and checks the meaning by asking.

subtype: Reading a speaker's gestures for meaning [Interpreting]
passage: In the science room in Istanbul, Pablo swept one hand in a wide curve above the desk. “The moon goes around the Earth like this,” he said. Zeynep watched the hand. It seemed to make a huge loop, then dip low, then rise. “Does the moon go up and down like a roller coaster?” she asked. Pablo laughed. “No, my hand wobbled. Thanks for asking.” He drew a circle on the board with the Earth in the middle. “Here. A steady round path.” Zeynep nodded. “Oh. It's more like a circle.”

qa.q: Where did the science lesson take place?
qa.a: It took place in the science room in Istanbul.

qa.q: What was Zeynep thinking when she asked if the moon goes up and down?
qa.a: She was trying to understand what she saw in his hand movement, which looked like a wobbly loop. She might have been a little unsure but willing to ask.

qa.q: What could Zeynep do when a gesture seems unclear?
qa.a: Ask a follow-up question, as she did, so the teacher can explain or draw it.

qa.q: What would change if Pablo had only used gestures and no board?
qa.a: Pupils might keep the wobbly picture of the moon's path, since gestures can clarify but also mislead. The drawing corrected it.

grounding: A pupil watches a teacher's hands describing a path and checks the meaning with a question.

passage: Divyansh was new in the colony, and Binita was walking him home from school. “Which way to your house?” he asked. Binita couldn't find the words, so she traced the road in the air with one finger: a long straight line, then a little hook, then a wide curve. “Ah, the hook is the sweet shop!” said Divyansh. “And the curve goes round the park.” Binita nodded, surprised. “Yes! Turn right at the sweet shop, and left after the park.” The words came easily after the gesture, as if her hand had found them first.

qa.q: What did Binita trace in the air?
qa.a: She traced the road in the air with one finger.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when she could not find the words, and what did her gesture do?
qa.a: She was probably a bit stuck and unsure how to explain. Tracing the road helped her sort out the route, and the words came easily after.

qa.q: What could an adult do to help a child explaining a route?
qa.a: Let the child gesture and ask what the hook or curve stands for, so the gesture can help the child think.

qa.q: How might Divyansh find Binita's gesture compared with words?
qa.a: Easier to follow, since he could work out the sweet shop and the park from the shapes. He was new and probably glad to get a clear picture.

grounding: A child traces a map in the air to explain the way home; gesture helps thought and explanation.

passage:
“Dhruv, how did the ball end up in Mrs Pai's garden?” asked Manoj, his father.
“It went like this.” Dhruv drew a circle in the air with his finger. “It hit the shed wall and came back and then, whoosh, up.”
“Show me again slowly.”
Dhruv traced it once more, frowning. “Oh! It hit the shed roof first. That's why it went the wrong way.”
“So it bounced off the roof.”
“Yes!”
Manoj smiled and let him keep moving his hands. “I'll go and say sorry to Mrs Pai. Want to come?”

qa.q: Whose garden did the ball end up in?
qa.a: It ended up in Mrs Pai's garden.

qa.q: What was Dhruv thinking when he traced the ball's path a second time?
qa.a: He was working out what really happened, and the tracing helped him realise the ball hit the shed roof first. He was probably a little worried about the trouble.

qa.q: What did Manoj do that helped Dhruv explain?
qa.a: He asked him to show it again slowly and let him keep moving his hands, so Dhruv could work out the route himself.

qa.q: How might Mrs Pai feel about the ball, and what would Manoj's visit change?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised or annoyed by the ball in her garden, and an apology would show that the family cares. She may also just be glad to know what happened.

grounding: A child traces a ball's path in the air to explain it, and gesturing helps the child work out the idea.

passage: It was pouring, and the bus to the fair would leave in ten minutes. Ojas ran into his house with Harish behind him, both soaked. Ojas's grandmother came into the room. Ojas quickly bent and touched her feet, as he did each time. Harish, whose family did not do this, froze. He glanced at the clock and at her. Then he stood straight and joined his palms. “Namaste, Dadi.” She nodded warmly, patted his cheek and said, “Both are good. Go, go, the bus won't wait.” They ran out into the rain, laughing.

qa.q: How many minutes until the bus to the fair left?
qa.a: The bus would leave in ten minutes.

qa.q: What might Harish have been feeling when he froze, and what else might explain it?
qa.a: Probably unsure what to do, since his family does not touch feet, and rushed because of the bus. He may also have wanted to be respectful without copying wrongly.

qa.q: How did Ojas's grandmother handle the moment?
qa.a: She accepted Harish's namaste warmly and said both ways are good, so nobody felt wrong, and she sent them on their way.

qa.q: How might Ojas see Harish's greeting?
qa.a: As just a different family way, since they went off laughing and Ojas seems to see no problem.

grounding: Kneeling or touching feet is respect in some families and not others; different greetings can both be respectful.

passage: On her first day at the new school, Vasudha stayed in her seat when Parul Ma'am walked in. The rest of the class stood up and said, “Good morning, Ma'am.” Vasudha's cheeks went hot. She stood late, halfway. Parul Ma'am smiled and said, “In your old school it was probably different. Here we stand to greet the teacher. It isn't about being small, it is our way of saying hello.” At recess her new friend Sarika said, “You'll get used to it.” Next morning Vasudha was the first to stand.

qa.q: What did the class do when Parul Ma'am walked in?
qa.a: They stood up and said, “Good morning, Ma'am.”

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she stayed in her seat and then stood late?
qa.a: Embarrassed and unsure, since her cheeks went hot. She was also probably trying to learn a new custom.

qa.q: What did Parul Ma'am do that helped Vasudha?
qa.a: She stayed kind and explained that standing is a way of saying hello here, not a sign of being small, and she acknowledged that Vasudha's old school may be different.

qa.q: How might the other children have seen Vasudha staying seated?
qa.a: Possibly as surprising, but they may also just have thought she was new. Sarika's friendly words suggest they were welcoming.

grounding: Standing to greet a teacher is respect in that school culture; customs differ across schools and families.

subtype: Slouching and sitting up in class [Interpreting]
passage: In the classroom of the village school, Anand slid down in his seat with his cheek on his hand, eyes half shut, while Disha Ma'am talked about fractions. Disha Ma'am's mouth tightened. He's bored, or he doesn't care, she thought. She walked over and asked quietly, “Anand, are you all right?” He blinked. “Sorry, Ma'am. We were up all night. The buffalo had her calf.” Disha Ma'am's face softened. “Congratulations. Have some water and sit up when you can. We'll go through the fractions again after break.”

qa.q: What happened at Anand's home during the night?
qa.a: The buffalo had her calf.

qa.q: What did Disha Ma'am first think Anand's slouching meant, and what did it turn out to be?
qa.a: She first thought he was bored or did not care. It turned out he was tired from being up all night with the buffalo.

qa.q: What did Disha Ma'am do that treated the posture as a clue rather than proof?
qa.a: She walked over and asked quietly if he was all right, and then offered water and a chance to go through the fractions again.

qa.q: How might Anand have felt when Disha Ma'am came over?
qa.a: Perhaps worried that he was in trouble, and then relieved when she softened. He was probably tired and glad to explain.

grounding: Slouching in class may show tiredness rather than boredom; posture is a clue, not proof of attitude.

subtype: Slouching and sitting up in class [Interpreting]
passage: In Ms Layla's class in Lisbon, Sofia slumped in her chair with her chin on her hand, staring at the ceiling. “Sit up, Sofia,” said Ms Layla. “We are learning about rivers.” Sofia straightened, but her eyes stayed on the ceiling. Ms Layla waited. After a moment Sofia said, “The river doesn't always flow to the sea. Sometimes it flows into a bigger river.” Ms Layla raised her eyebrows. “Yes. Good thinking.” Sofia looked pleased. “I think better when I lean.”

qa.q: What was Ms Layla teaching about?
qa.a: She was teaching about rivers.

qa.q: What did Ms Layla probably think about Sofia's slouch at first, and what else did it mean?
qa.a: She probably thought Sofia was not paying attention. It turned out Sofia was thinking hard, and she said she thinks better when she leans.

qa.q: What could Ms Layla do next time she sees a slouch?
qa.a: Give a little time or ask a question first, since posture is a clue and not proof of attitude.

qa.q: How might Sofia feel about being told to sit up?
qa.a: Perhaps a bit misunderstood, since she was thinking. She still answered politely and seemed pleased when praised.

grounding: Slouching can be a comfortable way of thinking; posture is a clue, not proof of attitude.

subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
passage: Farida paced up and down the corridor outside the science room, back and forth, her hands swinging. The test would start in five minutes. Nandini watched her from the bench. “Are you nervous?” “A bit,” said Farida. “But I'm also bursting with energy. I can't sit still.” Nandini nodded. “Want to walk to the water cooler and back with me?” They walked fast, and Farida stopped swinging her hands. When the bell rang, she sat down at her desk and took a deep breath. Her leg still bounced a little, but she began to write.

qa.q: Where did Farida pace before the test?
qa.a: She paced up and down the corridor outside the science room.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling as she paced, and what else does it show?
qa.a: A mix of nerves and extra energy, since she said she was a bit nervous but also bursting with energy. Moving helped her settle.

qa.q: What small step helped Farida focus before the test?
qa.a: Nandini offered a brisk walk to the water cooler and back, so the energy had somewhere to go before she sat.

qa.q: How might Nandini see Farida's pacing?
qa.a: She wondered if it was nerves, so she asked instead of assuming, and offered help. She may feel glad to be a support.

grounding: Pacing before a test can show nerves, excitement or a need for movement; movement helps focus.

subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
passage:
“Sit still, Santosh,” said Lalit Mama, looking up from his newspaper. “Your leg is shaking the whole table.”
“I am sitting still.”
“Your leg is bouncing. Are you doing it to annoy me?”
“No. It helps me think. My head gets stuck otherwise.”
Lalit Mama put the paper down. “Hmm. Stuck how?”
“Like sums go slow.”
“Then do ten jumps in the yard, come back and try again. And bounce the leg if it helps, but under the table.”
Santosh grinned. “Okay!”

qa.q: What did Lalit Mama say Santosh's leg was doing to the table?
qa.a: He said it was shaking the whole table.

qa.q: Why was Santosh bouncing his leg, and how did Lalit Mama first read it?
qa.a: He said it helps him think because his head gets stuck otherwise. Lalit Mama first wondered if he was doing it to annoy him.

qa.q: What could help Santosh focus on his sums?
qa.a: A short movement break, such as the ten jumps in the yard Lalit Mama suggested, and permission to bounce the leg quietly under the table.

qa.q: How might Lalit Mama feel when he hears Santosh's reason?
qa.a: Probably a bit surprised and glad he asked, and less annoyed once he understood. He then offered a practical fix.

grounding: Leg bouncing can show a need for movement rather than defiance; movement breaks help focus.
